solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Need brought back the old manservant

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a need is a lack of something
ye is the archaic spelling of the, as in Ye Olde Tea Shoppe

explanation.surface: Someone missing the old manservant who has finally been brought back into service.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the archaic article is turned round; the noun for a need stays as it is and goes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A lackey is a servant in livery, a footman, hence any servile attendant or manservant.

clue.text: Part of jacket displayed by mimic visiting Lakes

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's place, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for lake, doubled for the plural
to ape is to mimic

explanation.surface: An impressionist on a trip to the Lake District shows off some part of a jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: Doubling a single-letter abbreviation makes a plural, as pp for pages; here the two Ls flank the mimic.
explanation.definitionFit: The lapel is the folded-back flap on the front of a jacket below the collar.

clue.text: Vehicle family member used to carry black gemstone

indicators.note: whatever carries something holds it, so the pair of pieces holds a letter between them

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
an uncle is a relative

explanation.surface: A relative uses the car to transport a black jewel.
explanation.walkthrough: The car and the uncle together carry the black between them, so the abbreviation lands at the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbuncle is a red gem, typically a garnet cut in a rounded domed shape without facets.

clue.text: Issue primarily engaging American university

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.surface: A topic that mainly concerns an American college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a noun meaning a topic, but it is the verb meaning to send out.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to send out or give off, and to issue likewise means to put forth or discharge.

clue.text: They may be given work at last? Nonsense

definitions.text: They may be given work at last

blocks.clueFragment: They may be given work at last
blocks.note: first meaning: shoe menders, who work on a last, the foot-shaped block for shaping shoes
second meaning: British slang for rubbish, from rhyming slang

explanation.surface: Someone scoffing at the idea that workers will finally be given jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last' reads as finally, but a last is the shoemaker's foot-shaped mould. The slang word comes from rhyming slang, cobblers' awls, and is a mild British exclamation of disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoe repairers are tradesmen working at a last, and in British slang the same plural word means utter rubbish or tosh.

clue.text: Moving me a lot, a greyish yellow colour

indicators.note: things that move change position, so these letters shift into a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A drab colour that someone finds deeply touching.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'a' belongs to the letters being rearranged, not to the definition, which is easy to miss after the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatmeal names a pale fawn shade, the colour of ground oats, used for fabrics and paint.

clue.text: Swelling family, his, confused like yokels

indicators.note: something confused is mixed up, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: a bump is a swelling
kin are family
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man's growing family seems as muddled as country folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swelling family' reads as a growing household, but the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumpkin is an unsophisticated rustic, so behaving in that manner is like a yokel or country hick.

clue.text: Additional outlet, one no longer used by gunners

indicators.note: something no longer used has been dropped, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: an exit is a way out
the Roman numeral for one, which is removed
RA is the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners

explanation.surface: A spare exit point that the artillery no longer bothers with.
explanation.walkthrough: The one removed is the letter I, Roman one, taken out of the way out; the gunners then follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra and additional are synonyms, both meaning more than is usual or expected.

clue.text: Litter, perhaps? It’s a lie

blocks.note: first meaning: a frame for carrying a sick person, of which a litter is an example
second meaning: an exaggeration, a tall story

explanation.surface: Someone protesting that a claim about rubbish is untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' suggests rubbish or a batch of puppies, but here it is a carrying frame for the injured. The second sense is an old informal word for a fib that stretches the truth.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter carries patients like an ambulance frame, and an untruth that stretches the facts is informally called the same word.

clue.text: Region in which to practise matricide?

blocks.note: to kill your mother is, in slang
taken as written, completing the slang phrase for killing

explanation.surface: Asking which territory would be the place for murdering one's mother.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as DO MA IN: to do someone in is slang for to kill them, and ma is mother.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain is a territory or realm ruled over by someone, hence any region or sphere.

clue.text: Left in charge of old colonnade

blocks.note: port is the left side of a ship
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone left responsible for an ancient row of columns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as a verb, abandoned, but it is the nautical side; 'of' simply joins the last abbreviation on.
explanation.definitionFit: A portico is a porch or walkway roofed and supported by a row of columns at a building's entrance.

clue.text: Satan, possibly, ultimately cast in wax?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a wax is an old British word for a fit of anger, a temper
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a figure of the devil was finally moulded in wax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast in wax' suggests a sculpture, but wax here is the old sense of a rage, as in to be in a wax.
explanation.definitionFit: Satan is the devil who lures people into sin, one example of a seducer; 'possibly' flags the example.

clue.text: Hooligan’s fate blocked by university

indicators.note: something blocked has an obstacle lodged in it, so a letter sits inside

blocks.note: one's lot is one's fate
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A troublemaker's future ruined because a college stood in the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking definition to wordplay, not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A lout is a rough, aggressive young man, a yob, much the same as a hooligan.

clue.text: Turks are confused about a high-class pickled cabbage

indicators.note: confused things are muddled, so these letters are mixed up
about means around, so these letters surround another piece

blocks.note: the letters taken as written
taken as written
U means upper-class, a British usage

explanation.surface: Turkish diners baffled by a posh dish of preserved cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U, the British labels for posh and common speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauerkraut is the German dish of finely shredded cabbage fermented in brine, so it is cabbage that has been pickled.

clue.text: Blow from right or left initially endangering rock snake

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letters are taken

blocks.note: a wind blowing across from either flank
the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A punch thrown from either side that might threaten a rock snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like a punch, and 'rock snake' like the definition, but blow is a wind and rock only gives its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The sidewinder is a small desert rattlesnake of North America that moves by throwing its body sideways.

clue.text: Like a minority group’s undertaking blocking river

indicators.note: a blockage lodges inside a channel, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall
an action is something undertaken

explanation.surface: A small group's project dams a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay. The Fal is a short river in Cornwall, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A faction is a dissenting minority within a larger body, so the adjective describes anything relating to such a clique.

clue.text: Manhandle prisoner finally in thick mist on border

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the last letter is kept
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: fog is thick mist
the closing letter of the word
a march is a frontier region, as in the Welsh Marches

explanation.surface: Guards roughly bundling a captive away through dense fog at a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: March as a border is old but alive in the Welsh Marches, the borderland between England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: To frogmarch someone is to force them forward with arms pinned behind, a rough way of handling a captive.

clue.text: Girl from Dublin I am hugging?

indicators.note: taken from means extracted out of, so the letters are drawn out of the run of words

blocks.note: the run straddles the last letter of the city, the two short words, and the first of the verb

explanation.surface: An Irish girl announcing that she is giving someone a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'from Dublin' does double duty: it tells you where to look, and also that the name is Irish. It is pronounced Neeve.
explanation.definitionFit: Niamh is a common Irish female given name, borne by a goddess in Irish legend.

clue.text: Chaps in hail holding up a contract

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
in a down entry whatever holds something up lies beneath it, so one piece follows the other

blocks.note: taken as written
to hail someone is to greet them
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Men stuck out in a hailstorm delaying a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hail' suggests weather but is the verb to greet; 'holding up' suggests delay but places the wordplay beneath the single letter in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A contract is a binding agreement between parties, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Recipients of award, initially enervated and overweight

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: OBEs, people appointed Officers of the Order of the British Empire
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Honours recipients described as sluggish and too heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE is a British honour; people holding it are called OBEs, giving a plural abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means very fat, carrying excess body weight to a medically unhealthy degree.

clue.text: One who cherishes the person holding the purse strings?

definitions.text: the person holding the purse strings

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who treasures something, a literal agent noun

blocks.clueFragment: the person holding the purse strings
blocks.note: second meaning: the official in charge of an organisation's funds

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests loving whoever controls the money; the question mark flags that the first meaning is a coined literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as an agent noun, the word names one who prizes something, and conventionally it is the officer managing an organisation's finances.

clue.text: Costume head of tennis used to secure success?

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
a win is a success
to set something is to fix it firmly in place

explanation.surface: A tennis star's outfit chosen to ensure a victory.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis setting suggests set as a scoring unit, and in tennis a set is indeed what you win, which the question mark nods to.
explanation.definitionFit: A twinset is a matching cardigan and jumper worn together, a classic British women's outfit, so an ensemble or costume.

clue.text: Justice threw in sponge in Ely, losing heart

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
the heart of a word is its middle, so the central letter goes

blocks.note: the cathedral city with its middle letter dropped
to throw in the sponge, like throwing in the towel, is to give up

explanation.surface: A judge who gave up while in Ely, losing the will to go on.
explanation.walkthrough: Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England; throwing in the sponge is the boxing corner's sign of surrender.
explanation.definitionFit: Equity is fairness and impartiality, and also the body of law that supplements common law, both close to justice.

clue.text: Wine that French accumulated in Caribbean island

blocks.note: Martini is a brand of vermouth, a fortified wine
que is French for that

explanation.surface: French wine stockpiled on a Caribbean island.
explanation.walkthrough: Martini as wine is a stretch, since it is now mostly a cocktail, but the brand is a vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Martinique is a French overseas island in the Lesser Antilles of the eastern Caribbean Sea.

clue.text: Country artist breaking law endlessly

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it
without an end means the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a rule is a law, with its final letter gone
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A country-music performer who keeps on breaking the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country artist' looks like a single phrase about a musician, but 'Country' alone is the definition, used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Country used adjectivally, as in country life, means of the countryside, which is what rural means.

clue.text: Broadcaster from east or west?

blocks.note: surface reading: a radio or TV station based in the East or the West
setter's reading: the nickname reads the same whichever end of the across entry you start from

explanation.surface: Asking whether a radio station is from the Orient or the West.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beeb is an informal British nickname for the BBC, the British Broadcasting Corporation; east and west stand for the two directions of reading across the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC is Britain's national public broadcaster, popularly known by this affectionate shortened nickname.

clue.text: Fellow joining club to exercise in water

indicators.note: to join something is to attach onto it, so one piece is tacked onto the other

blocks.note: a bat is a club used in games like cricket
he refers to a male, a fellow

explanation.surface: A man signing up at a club so he can do aqua aerobics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' looks like a sports club to join, but it is a bat; the fellow joins on after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To bathe, in British usage, is to swim or take a dip in the sea or a river for pleasure and exercise.

clue.text: Joint head of kindergarten born in Marseille

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
née is French for born, as used for maiden names

explanation.surface: A nursery school's joint principal who was born in Marseille.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint head' reads as a co-principal; Marseille just tells you to use French.
explanation.definitionFit: The knee is the hinge joint between thigh and lower leg, one example of a body joint.

clue.text: Extremely rare, brightly coloured, very large screen

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
red is a vivid colour
OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: A huge colourful screen of a kind hardly ever seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely rare' looks like an intensifier but takes the outer letters. OS, outsize, is a British clothing label.
explanation.definitionFit: A reredos is an ornamental panel or partition behind a church altar, a decorative screen.

clue.text: Function a new group initiated in shelter

indicators.note: to initiate is to begin, so only the opening letter is taken
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a tent is a shelter
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A party with a fresh group of members inducted under canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' suggests a party or role, but it is the mathematical sense; 'initiated' looks like inducted but just takes a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangent is one of the trigonometric functions, alongside sine and cosine, in mathematics.

clue.text: It interrupts a term at Oxford, engendering much mirth

indicators.note: something that interrupts breaks into the middle, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Hilary is the spring term at Oxford University
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something disrupting an Oxford term causes great amusement.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford's terms are Michaelmas, Hilary and Trinity; Hilary runs from January to March.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilarity is boisterous merriment and loud laughter, a great deal of amusement.

clue.text: Observe article, and fume!

blocks.note: to see is to observe
the definite article

explanation.surface: Read a newspaper piece and get angry!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper item, but it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: To seethe is to be inwardly furious, boiling with anger, which is what fuming means.
